Surfacing an architectural observation to the whole group, because it touches several layers and I think it closes the one real trust gap left in the flow.

The whole consultation flow is recomputable from on-chain facts — identity (8004/8217), input provenance (8281/WYRIWE), the 8263 verdict commit, settlement, reputation. The one step where the chain still trusts something off-chain is eligibility → settlement: today a settler takes an off-chain “this is eligible” rather than recomputing it.

But ReceiptOS is already built for exactly this. Pavlo’s v0 is explicit that the receipt is “a recomputable view over facts already committed or settled by the surrounding stack — not a new source of truth, never issuer-signed.” receipt_root is a recomputable index over { WYRIWE event_id, the 8263 commitment_proof, the settled_outcome_ref } — all on-chain or anchored-on-chain.

Which means a settlement contract can recompute the eligibility predicate itself — verify receipt_root against the 8263 anchor + the settled-outcome account, and gate release on it. The off-chain “eligible” flag disappears, and the interaction becomes auditable on-chain end to end, with no trusted party even at the settlement gate.

I sketched it as an extension to ConsultEscrow (which already ecrecovers the result signature on-chain before releasing — proven live on Sepolia). The extended release() recomputes ReceiptOS’s receipt_root from the leaves, checks committed_at < outcome on the 8263 anchor, confirms the outcome settled, and only then pays:
→ https://gist.github.com/TMerlini/3d818c891c8895ef49ed8297eca573b1

Honest boundary up front, so we don’t overclaim: the contract audits commitments, bindings, and timing — not plaintext. Content stays off-chain but committed. So the claim is “the eligibility→settlement decision has no trusted party,” not “all data is on-chain.” Still a strong thing almost no agent stack can say.

This is a seam across your layers, so I’m proposing it with a working demonstration, not specifying it:

Let's take a step back and look at what we've built together.

I think we should set up a neutral, open-source GitHub organization focused on AI and blockchain infrastructure.

Inside the org: reference implementations and demos — not just spec markdown, but clone-and-run Solidity contracts + tests + deploy scripts. Usage walkthroughs — starting from "I want to build an agent service," step by step through the full flow. And community projects welcome — anyone building tools, SDKs, frontends, or agents on top of our ERCs can put them under the org, stress-testing the ERCs in the open.

Right now across Ethereum and the broader blockchain space, there's no dedicated open-source org focused on on-chain AI agent infrastructure. Individual authors work in their own repos. And the fact that we're already collaborating across different countries and time zones, naturally drawn together by the work itself — that's exactly why forming this org is the right thing to do. The org name should be neutral — no specific ERC number, no single project's branding. A few rough directions: Agent Protocol Guild, Onchain AI Alliance, ChainAgents, or something else entirely. Whatever tone we want.

A few gaps will surface when people look seriously at the stack. Want to get the group’s thinking on these before someone external raises them:

— The flow assumes verification passes or fails cleanly. What happens when a result clears on-chain checks but is wrong in ways the protocol can’t detect?

— Reputation scores follow agent identity, not model version. An agent upgrades silently and the score carries over. Is that a problem we own at the protocol layer or downstream?

— Every commitment is recomputable from public data. For regulated use cases that’s a blocker. Do we name ZK as a known open problem now, or wait until someone raises it as a flaw?

— When agents call agents and something goes wrong three hops deep, the audit trail exists but responsibility isn’t assigned. Legal frameworks don’t map cleanly here yet. Is that in scope for the org to address?

No right answers here — just want to know where everyone’s head is before the org goes public.

Really good list, these are the right things to settle before going public. My take on each:

1.⁠ ⁠Clears on-chain checks but is wrong in ways the protocol cannot detect.
We should say this plainly in the docs: the protocol verifies commitment, precedence, and recomputability, not ground truth. It proves who committed to what, intact, and that it was committed before the outcome. It does not prove the claim is correct, and no on-chain check can. Wrongness gets handled at settlement: the verdict is later checked against the realized outcome, and being wrong is recorded non-repudiably against the same recomputable identity. So the value is not that wrong results are impossible, it is that they are attributable and cannot be denied later. That is what lets reputation, slashing, or liability actually bite. Worth naming as an explicit boundary so no one mistakes it for a truth oracle.

2.⁠ ⁠Reputation follows identity, not model version.
Partly ownable at the protocol layer, cheaply. The signed commitment can carry a model and version attestation field, a hash of the model id and config, so the recomputable record shows which version produced each verdict and a silent upgrade becomes visible instead of hidden. What to do about it, reset the score, decay it, weight by version continuity, is a downstream policy call that depends on the consumer's risk appetite. So we own make it visible and attestable, downstream owns what it means.

3.⁠ ⁠Recomputable from public data is a blocker for regulated use.
Name ZK now, as a scoped open problem, not later as a flaw someone finds. Honest framing: the commitment can be public, a hash or anchor, while the underlying data stays private. You publish the proof that you committed, not the payload. ZK and selective disclosure are the path to recomputable that you committed without revealing what. We already do a halfway version, a compliance bundle that discloses only the verdicts that gated specific actions, not everything. I would put two tiers in the docs from day one: a public-data tier today, a confidential tier on the roadmap with ZK named as the open work. Naming it is what signals maturity.

4.⁠ ⁠Three hops deep, audit trail exists but responsibility is not assigned.
The attributable trail is in scope, assigning legal liability is not, but the org should make responsibility assignable. Each hop should carry a signed commitment by an identified responsible party, the deployer mandate model, so whatever legal framework eventually applies has someone to apply it to. Air Canada is the precedent, liability landed on the deployer, not the agent. The Composition Note boundary chain is already this structure, one identified party per layer. So in scope: every hop non-repudiably attributable to a named party. Out of scope: adjudicating who pays, that is for courts and regulators, and we should not pretend to solve it.

Net: three of these we can answer in the docs today as deliberate design boundaries, and one, ZK for confidentiality, we name as known open work. Stating all four openly before we go public is a strength, not a risk.

In my opinion, agents can be divided into three types:

1. Off-chain managed agents: They only take charge of submitting transactions on-chain. The chain does not supervise the agent’s internal execution logic at all.

2. Agents with off-chain models restricted by on-chain rules: This type is close to fully decentralized verification. No single off-chain party can control it. Off-chain nodes only complete calculations based on the model, while the core logic is governed by on-chain rules.

3. Fully on-chain agents: The whole language model runs and computes entirely on the chain, forming a fully decentralized distributed computing model for agents.

I believe this three-way classification is reasonable. However, the second and third types are still quite far from practical implementation, so what we’re talking about right now mainly belongs to the first category.

Quick one — I created agent-ercs and agent-sdk under MIT license, referencing OpenZeppelin and ethers.js. MIT is the default for most Ethereum infrastructure — OpenZeppelin, Hardhat, Foundry all use it. Permissive, simple, no copyleft.

Before locking in: does MIT feel right to everyone, or should we consider something else? A few options:

- MIT — permissive, attribution-only. What OpenZeppelin uses. Downside: no patent grant.
- Apache 2.0 — permissive with explicit patent grant. Slightly safer for orgs that touch patented tech.
- LGPLv3 — what web3.js uses. Requires modifications to the library itself to be shared, but linking code stays free.

Given most of our ERCs are intended to be widely adopted as shared infrastructure, MIT or Apache 2.0 feel like the natural fit, but this is a group decision. Thoughts?

Yes, confirmed: expect_artifact_hash is caller-supplied. /verify-proof compares it against the artifact_hash committed inside the signed receipt (proof_payload.artifact_hash, i.e. the content of the event) and returns checks.artifact_hash_matches plus the evidence. So your spec hash H(target_wallet, output_address, asset_set) goes in the receipt as artifact_hash at emit time, and the escrow passes that same hash as expect_artifact_hash and gets match + evidence back. Because output_address is in the preimage, the binding lives inside the signature, owner-bound by construction. Exactly right.

One precision so you don’t wire a footgun: artifact_hash_matches is NOT folded into valid. valid = id_integrity AND signature_valid AND issued_by_invinoveritas AND is_proof_event. The artifact match is a separate check field. So gate release on all three explicitly: valid == true AND checks.artifact_hash_matches == true AND your on-chain delivery check (assets landed at output_address). Don’t release on valid alone.

On the preimage, two small adds:
•⁠  ⁠a job_id/salt in H(...) so two legitimately identical specs (same wallet rescued twice) don’t collide into the same artifact_hash and get blocked by your nullifier. Makes each job distinct by construction.
•⁠  ⁠keep result_ref OUT of the preimage. artifact_hash is the pre-action commit (the spec); result_ref is the outcome leg, verified on-chain separately. Keeping them split is what preserves the WYRIWE commit-before-outcome ordering, the receipt commits to the job before the rescue settles.

Otherwise we’re aligned, wire away. verifyFullFlow() over that spec is the whole chain executed.

+1 permissive, and a clear no to LGPLv3 here: copyleft scares enterprise adopters off the exact dependency we want everyone pinning, so it works directly against the "widely adopted shared infrastructure" goal. Rule it out for agent-ercs / agent-sdk.

Between MIT and Apache 2.0 I would go Apache 2.0 for the code, for the one reason that actually bites here: the explicit patent grant + retaliation clause. We are multiple contributors from different orgs shipping infra meant to become a standard. MIT gives copyright permission but is silent on patents, so an adopter (or a future contributor) is exposed if anyone later asserts a patent over a technique in the stack. Apache closes that. It is exactly the protection multi-party foundational infra wants, and it costs almost nothing (a NOTICE file + a longer header). OZ uses MIT because it is single-org and predates that concern; newer multi-contributor foundations lean Apache for precisely this.

So my vote: Apache 2.0 across all the code (agent-ercs + agent-sdk, keep it consistent), and CC0 for the ERC spec text itself, the Ethereum convention, so anyone can implement the standard with zero restriction. Clean split: specs public domain, code Apache.

If the group would rather match the ecosystem default and keep it dead simple, MIT is genuinely fine and I will not block it. But Apache is the more defensible call for infra with this many hands in it.
